EMPLOYER LIABILITY FOR NEGLIGENT HIRING, SUPERVISION, AND RETENTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Home Services, Inc.

ABOUT THIS NEGLIGENT HIRING, SUPERVISION, AND RETENTION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the California common-law doctrine under which an employer may be directly liable to a third person for its own negligence in hiring, supervising, or retaining an employee who is incompetent or unfit, as distinct from the employer's vicarious liability (respondeat superior) for an employee's acts within the scope of employment. It states the general duty of ordinary care in Civil Code Section 1714, the Restatement (Second) of Agency Section 213 rule that California courts follow, the knew-or-should-have-known standard and the requirement that the employer's knowledge relate to the particular risk that materialized, the rule that the employee's fitness is measured against the specific work to be performed, the direct (not vicarious) character of the liability, the end of the duty when employment ends, the effect of an employer's admission of vicarious liability, the application of the doctrine to public entities through Government Code Section 815.2, and the two-year limitations period of Code of Civil Procedure Section 335.1. Acme Home Services, Inc. has described the position or positions to which this sheet relates, including the degree of contact the work involves with customers, clients, minors, patients, or other third persons, as follows: In-home repair technicians who enter customers' residences unaccompanied. Acme Home Services, Inc. has described its pre-hire screening and post-hire supervision practices, if any, as follows: Reference checks and a consumer-report background check after a conditional offer; ride-along supervision during the first 30 days. Other documents in this corpus separately describe statutory limits on what an employer may ask about or consider in an applicant's criminal history (the Fair Chance Act and Labor Code Section 432.7), the consumer-report and investigative-consumer-report disclosure rules, and Live Scan fingerprint background checks; those limits are not restated here. This document states the content of the statutes and published case law as of the date checked; it does not determine whether any particular hiring, supervision, or retention decision was negligent, whether any particular harm was foreseeable, or whether any particular screening step was or was not required, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice or for consulting a licensed attorney.

THE GENERAL DUTY OF ORDINARY CARE (CIVIL CODE SECTION 1714)
Civil Code Section 1714, subdivision (a), states California's general rule of negligence liability: everyone is responsible not only for the result of his or her willful acts but also for an injury occasioned to another by his or her want of ordinary care or skill in the management of his or her property or person, except so far as the injured person has, willfully or by want of ordinary care, brought the injury upon himself or herself. The employer's direct liability for negligent hiring, supervision, or retention described in the other clauses of this document is an application of this general duty of ordinary care to the employer's own conduct in selecting and overseeing its employees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Everyone is responsible, not only for the result of his or her willful acts, but also for an injury occasioned to another by his or her want of ordinary care or skill in the management of his or her property or person, except so far as the latter has, willfully or by want of ordinary care, brought the injury upon himself or herself."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1714(a), Civ. Code § 1714(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1714.)
  Known gap: Section 1714(a) states the general duty only; it does not mention employers, hiring, or supervision, and the specific contours of the negligent-hiring doctrine come from case law quoted in the other clauses of this document. Subdivisions (b) through (d) of Section 1714, which concern the furnishing of alcoholic beverages and social-host liability, and the sentence of subdivision (a) concerning the design, distribution, or marketing of firearms and ammunition, are not restated here. The Restatement (Second) of Agency, which the courts cite as the source of the doctrine, is a secondary source that was not separately fetched for this document; its language is quoted only as reproduced in the published opinions.

CALIFORNIA RECOGNIZES NEGLIGENT HIRING AS AN INDEPENDENT GROUND OF EMPLOYER LIABILITY (RESTATEMENT SECOND OF AGENCY SECTION 213)
In Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church (1992), a case arising from a church's hiring of a youth director, later a pastor, who molested a child parishioner, the California Court of Appeal identified two lines of authority on "negligent hiring" and stated that California follows the view that an employer may be liable to a third person for negligently hiring an incompetent or unfit employee. The court stated that California follows the rule set forth in the Restatement Second of Agency Section 213, under which a person conducting an activity through servants or other agents is subject to liability for harm resulting from his conduct if he is negligent or reckless in the employment of improper persons or instrumentalities in work involving risk of harm to others. Quoting comment d to that section, the court reproduced the Restatement's statements that the principal may be negligent because he has reason to know that the agent, because of his qualities, is likely to harm others in view of the work entrusted to him, that liability results not because of the relation of the parties but because the employer antecedently had reason to believe that an undue risk of harm would exist because of the employment, and that if the work is likely to subject third persons to serious risk of great harm, there is a special duty of investigation. The court summarized the California rule as follows: an employer can be held liable for negligent hiring if he knows the employee is unfit, or has reason to believe the employee is unfit, or fails to use reasonable care to discover the employee's unfitness before hiring him. On the summary-judgment record, the court found a triable issue as to whether the church should have known of the youth director's history and reversed in part.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The other view, which California follows, is that an employer may be liable to a third person for negligently hiring an incompetent or unfit employee."
  — Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church, 8 Cal. App. 4th 828, 836 (1992) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2277473/evan-f-v-hughson-united-methodist-church/)
  "California follows the rule set forth in the Restatement Second of Agency section 213, which provides in pertinent part: “A person conducting an activity through servants or other agents is subject to liability for harm resulting from his conduct if he is negligent or reckless:"
  — Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church, 8 Cal. App. 4th 828, 836 (1992) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2277473/evan-f-v-hughson-united-methodist-church/)
  "the work is likely to subject third persons to serious risk of great harm, there is a special duty of investigation"
  — Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church, 8 Cal. App. 4th 828, 842 (1992) (quoting Rest.2d Agency, § 213, com. d) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2277473/evan-f-v-hughson-united-methodist-church/)
  "Accordingly, in California, an employer can be held liable for negligent hiring if he knows the employee is unfit, or has reason to believe the employee is unfit or fails to use reasonable care to discover the employee’s unfitness before hiring him."
  — Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church, 8 Cal. App. 4th 828, 843 (1992) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2277473/evan-f-v-hughson-united-methodist-church/)
  Known gap: Evan F. was decided on a summary-judgment record involving a religious employer and a position entrusted with the care of minors; the opinion also addressed a separate defendant (the church's regional conference), the scope-of-employment question, and other theories not restated here. The Restatement (Second) of Agency Section 213 and its comment d are quoted only as reproduced in the opinion; the Restatement itself was not separately fetched. The opinion's text, as published, contains spacing artifacts within its Restatement quotations (for example, "If. . .the work"), which are not reproduced in the quotation below; the quotation below begins after that fragment. The gendered pronouns in the quoted passages are preserved as written.

THE EMPLOYER'S KNOWLEDGE MUST RELATE TO THE PARTICULAR RISK THAT MATERIALIZED (DOE V. CAPITAL CITIES)
In Doe v. Capital Cities (1996), the California Court of Appeal affirmed the dismissal of a negligent hiring, training, and supervision claim brought by an aspiring actor who alleged he was drugged and sexually assaulted by a television network's casting director at the casting director's home. The court stated that California case law recognizes the theory that an employer can be liable to a third person for negligently hiring, supervising, or retaining an unfit employee, and that liability is based upon the facts that the employer knew or should have known that hiring the employee created a particular risk or hazard and that particular harm materializes. The complaint alleged that the employer knew or should have known that the casting director used serious, mind-altering illegal drugs, that he used his position to gain sexual favors, and that use of a "casting couch" is common in the entertainment industry. The court held those allegations insufficient: knowledge that the employee personally used drugs did not equate with knowledge that he would surreptitiously drug a prospective employee and violently assault him, and knowledge that he used his position to extract or coerce sexual favors was not knowledge of the type of conduct alleged. The same opinion separately held that the plaintiff had adequately pleaded a sexual harassment claim under the Fair Employment and Housing Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "California case law recognizes the theory that an employer can be liable to a third person for negligently hiring, supervising, or retaining an unfit employee."
  — Doe v. Capital Cities, 50 Cal. App. 4th 1038, 1054 (1996) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2292640/doe-v-capital-cities/)
  "Liability is based upon the facts that the employer knew or should have known that hiring the employee created a particular risk or hazard and that particular harm materializes."
  — Doe v. Capital Cities, 50 Cal. App. 4th 1038, 1054 (1996) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2292640/doe-v-capital-cities/)
  "ABC’s knowledge that Marshall personally used “serious mind-altering drugs” does not equate with knowledge that he would surreptitiously use drugs to place a prospective employee into a situation of helplessness before violently assaulting him."
  — Doe v. Capital Cities, 50 Cal. App. 4th 1038, 1054 (1996) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2292640/doe-v-capital-cities/)
  Known gap: Doe v. Capital Cities was decided on demurrer, so the court assessed only the sufficiency of the pleaded allegations; it did not decide what an employer must do to investigate an applicant, and it did not hold that an employer is never liable for an employee's off-premises or off-hours conduct. The opinion's separate FEHA sexual-harassment holding, and its discussion of the relationship between a job applicant and a prospective employer under FEHA, are not restated here. The quotations below are the opinion's own statements of the standard; the first two are frequently reproduced in later opinions (for example, Delfino v. Agilent Technologies and Phillips v. TLC Plumbing, quoted in other clauses of this document).

UNFITNESS IS MEASURED AGAINST THE SPECIFIC WORK TO BE PERFORMED (FEDERICO V. SUPERIOR COURT)
In Federico v. Superior Court (1997), the California Court of Appeal directed entry of summary judgment for the owner of a hairstyling college who had hired, without a background or reference check, a supervisor with two prior convictions for sexual offenses against young males; the supervisor later molested the minor son of a student after meeting him at the school. Assuming for purposes of review that the owner knew or should have known of the prior convictions and could have foreseen some contact with minors, the court held that hiring the supervisor did not, as a matter of law, breach the employer's limited duty to exercise reasonable care in selecting employees. The court explained that an employer's duty, as defined by California authority and the Restatement, is breached only when the employer knows, or should know, facts which would warn a reasonable person that the employee presents an undue risk of harm to third persons in light of the particular work to be performed. It distinguished Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church on the ground that the pastor there was hired into roles that regularly entrusted him with the care and supervision of minors, whereas the supervisor's position at the hairstyling college required him only to supervise adult students and perform administrative tasks. The court stated that an employer is not charged with guaranteeing the safety of anyone its employee might incidentally meet while on the job against injuries inflicted independent of the performance of work-related functions, and that liability can be imposed only when the employer knows, or should know, that the employee, because of past behavior or other factors, is unfit for the specific tasks to be performed. The court also rejected a negligent-supervision theory because there was no showing that the incidents relied on had been called to the employer's attention or that the employer should have suspected inappropriate behavior on the job.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "an employer’s duty, as defined by California authority and the Restatement, is breached only when the employer knows, or should know, facts which would warn a reasonable person that the employee presents an undue risk of harm to third persons in light of the particular work to be performed."
  — Federico v. Superior Court, 59 Cal. App. 4th 1207, 1214 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2243921/federico-v-superior-court/)
  "An employer is not charged with guaranteeing the safety of anyone his employee might incidentally meet while on the job against injuries inflicted independent of the performance of work-related functions. Rather, as we have previously explained, liability for negligence can be imposed only when the employer knows, or should know, that the employee, because of past behavior or other factors, is unfit for the specific tasks to be performed."
  — Federico v. Superior Court, 59 Cal. App. 4th 1207, 1215 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2243921/federico-v-superior-court/)
  "the contrast between the facts in Evan F. and the present case highlights the significance of the Restatement’s proviso that an employer’s liability must be determined in the context of the specific duties the work entails."
  — Federico v. Superior Court, 59 Cal. App. 4th 1207, 1215 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2243921/federico-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: Federico was decided by writ of mandate on a summary-judgment record and turned on the specific duties of the position at issue; the opinion expressly assumed, without deciding, the employer's knowledge of the prior convictions. The opinion does not address statutory limits on an employer's consideration of criminal history (Labor Code Section 432.7 and the Fair Chance Act, adopted after this decision), which are covered elsewhere in the corpus. The Restatement (Second) of Agency Section 213 and comment d are quoted in the opinion as reproduced from Roman Catholic Bishop v. Superior Court, 42 Cal.App.4th 1556 (1996), which was not separately fetched for this document. The gendered pronoun in the second quotation is preserved as written.

NEGLIGENT SUPERVISION AND RETENTION IS DIRECT LIABILITY REQUIRING EMPLOYER KNOWLEDGE AND CAUSATION (DELFINO V. AGILENT TECHNOLOGIES)
In Delfino v. Agilent Technologies, Inc. (2006), the California Court of Appeal affirmed summary judgment for an employer whose employee had used the employer's computer system to send anonymous threats over the Internet. Restating the standard from Roman Catholic Bishop v. Superior Court, Doe v. Capital Cities, and Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church, the court stated that liability for negligent supervision and/or retention of an employee is one of direct liability for negligence, not vicarious liability. The negligent supervision and retention theory failed for three reasons: it was doubtful, under the factors of Rowland v. Christian, that the employer owed the plaintiffs a duty; even assuming a duty, there was no evidence the employer breached it, because the employer had no knowledge of the content of the employee's threatening messages or of his use of the company system to send them until after the fact, and its internal investigations had not uncovered that use; and even assuming knowledge and inaction, there was no evidence the employee used the employer's system to threaten the plaintiffs after the employer could have acted, so any negligent supervision or retention was not the cause of the claimed injuries.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Liability for negligent supervision and/or retention of an employee is one of direct liability for negligence, not vicarious liability."
  — Delfino v. Agilent Technologies, Inc., 145 Cal. App. 4th 790, 815 (2006) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2247530/delfino-v-agilent-technologies-inc/)
  "Second, even were we to assume the existence of a duty, there was no evidence that Agilent breached any duty of care with respect to the supervision or retention of Moore as an employee."
  — Delfino v. Agilent Technologies, Inc., 145 Cal. App. 4th 790, 817 (2006) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2247530/delfino-v-agilent-technologies-inc/)
  "Thus, any negligent supervision and/or retention of Moore by Agilent—which alleged negligence, as we have concluded, was devoid of factual support—was not the cause of plaintiffs’ claimed injuries."
  — Delfino v. Agilent Technologies, Inc., 145 Cal. App. 4th 790, 817 (2006) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2247530/delfino-v-agilent-technologies-inc/)
  Known gap: Delfino principally decided that the employer was immune under Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act as a provider of an interactive computer service, and also rejected ratification and respondeat superior theories; those holdings are not restated here. The court's duty analysis under Rowland v. Christian was expressed as doubt rather than a definitive holding. The decision concerned supervision and retention of an existing employee rather than the initial hiring decision, and its knowledge and causation reasoning is summarized here because the court treated the negligent hiring, supervision, and retention theories as governed by the same standard.

NO DUTY FOR HARM INFLICTED BY A FORMER EMPLOYEE AFTER EMPLOYMENT ENDS (PHILLIPS V. TLC PLUMBING)
In Phillips v. TLC Plumbing, Inc. (2009), the California Court of Appeal affirmed summary judgment for a plumbing company sued for negligent hiring and retention after a former service repairman shot and killed a customer he had first met on service calls while employed. The company's owner had learned at hiring that the repairman was on parole and had apparently been convicted of a domestic violence and/or arson offense; the company later terminated him, and the killing occurred about two years after termination. Finding no California case on point, the court surveyed decisions from other jurisdictions applying the Restatement Second of Agency and concluded that, because the employer-employee relationship ends on termination of employment, an employer does not owe a plaintiff a duty of care in a negligent hiring and retention action for harm inflicted by a former employee, even where the former employee initially met the plaintiff while employed. Because the tortious act occurred two years after the employment was terminated, the defendants owed no duty at the time of the act and could not be held liable on the negligent hiring and retention cause of action.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Because the employer-employee relationship ends on termination of an employee’s employment, we conclude an employer does not owe a plaintiff a duty of care in a negligent hiring and retention action for an injury or other harm inflicted by a former employee on the plaintiff even though that former employee, as in this case, initially met the plaintiff while employed by the employer."
  — Phillips v. TLC Plumbing, Inc., 172 Cal. App. 4th 1133, 1144 (2009) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2287828/phillips-v-tlc-plumbing-inc/)
  "because Cain’s tortious act on Judith occurred two years after his employment with TLC was terminated, Defendants did not owe Plaintiff a duty of care at the time of Cain’s tortious act and therefore cannot be held liable on a cause of action for negligent hiring and retention."
  — Phillips v. TLC Plumbing, Inc., 172 Cal. App. 4th 1133, 1145 (2009) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2287828/phillips-v-tlc-plumbing-inc/)
  Known gap: Phillips addressed only whether a duty existed for post-termination conduct; it did not decide whether the initial hiring or the retention of the employee during his employment was negligent, and the opinion offered additional, alternative grounds for the summary judgment that are not restated here. The decision does not address any duty an employer may have under other theories (for example, a duty to warn) and does not address harm inflicted during employment by an employee who is later terminated.

AN EMPLOYER'S ADMISSION OF VICARIOUS LIABILITY MAKES NEGLIGENT HIRING AND RETENTION CLAIMS IRRELEVANT (DIAZ V. CARCAMO)
In Diaz v. Carcamo (2011), the California Supreme Court reaffirmed its 1954 decision in Armenta v. Churchill and held that when a plaintiff injured by an employee's negligent driving sues the employer on both respondeat superior and negligent entrustment, hiring, or retention theories, and the employer admits vicarious liability for any negligent driving by its employee, the plaintiff may not continue to pursue the negligent entrustment, hiring, or retention claims. The court described the theory of negligent entrustment as making an employer liable for its own negligence in choosing an employee to drive a vehicle, and stated that an employer's admission of vicarious liability for its employee's negligence makes claims of negligent entrustment, hiring, or retention irrelevant, so that no reason exists to try such claims at all. The court rejected the Court of Appeal's view that this rule had been undermined by California's adoption of comparative fault and by Proposition 51, and it reversed a judgment in which the trial court had admitted evidence of the truck driver's prior accidents and employment history over the employer's objection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "The theory of negligent entrustment makes an employer liable for its own negligence in choosing an employee to drive a vehicle. If, as here, a plaintiff asserts both theories, and the employer admits vicarious liability for any negligent driving by its employee, can the plaintiff still pursue the negligent entrustment claim?"
  — Diaz v. Carcamo, 51 Cal. 4th 1148, 1152 (2011) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/844279/diaz-v-carcamo/)
  "an employer’s admission of vicarious liability for its employee’s negligence makes claims of negligent entrustment, hiring, or retention irrelevant. Thus, no reason exists to try such claims at all, whether separately from the negligence claim or at the same time."
  — Diaz v. Carcamo, 51 Cal. 4th 1148, 1158 (2011) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/844279/diaz-v-carcamo/)
  Known gap: Diaz arose from a motor-vehicle collision and addressed negligent entrustment, hiring, and retention claims that sought to impose on the employer the same liability as its employee's; the opinion does not address a case in which the employer's own negligence is alleged to have caused harm beyond the employee's negligence, and it does not address intentional torts by employees that fall outside the scope of employment (as in the cases quoted in other clauses of this document), where respondeat superior may be unavailable. The opinion's discussion of comparative fault, Proposition 51, and the specific evidence admitted at trial is not restated here.

PUBLIC ENTITIES: VICARIOUS LIABILITY FOR ADMINISTRATORS' NEGLIGENT HIRING, SUPERVISION, AND RETENTION (GOVERNMENT CODE SECTION 815.2; C.A. V. WILLIAM S. HART)
Government Code Section 815.2, subdivision (a), provides that a public entity is liable for injury proximately caused by an act or omission of an employee of the public entity within the scope of his employment if the act or omission would, apart from that section, have given rise to a cause of action against that employee. In C.A. v. William S. Hart Union High School District (2012), the California Supreme Court held that a public school district may be vicariously liable under Section 815.2 for the negligence of supervisory or administrative personnel who knew or should have known of a guidance counselor's propensities and nevertheless hired, retained, and inadequately supervised her; the court concluded that the plaintiff's theory of vicarious liability for negligent hiring, retention, and supervision was legally viable, reversing a dismissal on demurrer. The court emphasized that a district's liability must be based on evidence of negligent hiring, supervision, or retention, not on assumptions or speculation, and that an individual school employee's sexual misconduct with a student does not of itself establish, or raise any presumption, that the employing district should bear liability. The court also noted that even when an administrator's negligence is established, the greater share of fault will ordinarily lie with the individual who intentionally abused or harassed the student, which should be reflected in any allocation of comparative fault.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "A public entity is liable for injury proximately caused by an act or omission of an employee of the public entity within the scope of his employment if the act or omission would, apart from this section, have given rise to a cause of action against that employee or his personal representative."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 815.2(a), Gov. Code § 815.2(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=815.2.)
  "We conclude plaintiff’s theory of vicarious liability for negligent hiring, retention and supervision is a legally viable one."
  — C.A. v. William S. Hart Union High School District, 53 Cal. 4th 861, 865 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/844215/ca-v-william-s-hart-union-high-school-district/)
  "At the same time, we emphasize that a district’s liability must be based on evidence of negligent hiring, supervision or retention, not on assumptions or speculation. That an individual school employee has committed sexual misconduct with a student or students does not of itself establish, or raise any presumption, that the employing district should bear liability for the resulting injuries."
  — C.A. v. William S. Hart Union High School District, 53 Cal. 4th 861, 878 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/844215/ca-v-william-s-hart-union-high-school-district/)
  "Within these limits, we conclude a public school district may be vicariously liable under section 815.2 for the negligence of administrators or supervisors in hiring, supervising and retaining a school employee who sexually harasses and abuses a student."
  — C.A. v. William S. Hart Union High School District, 53 Cal. 4th 861, 879 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/844215/ca-v-william-s-hart-union-high-school-district/)
  Known gap: C.A. concerned a public school district and rested on the special relationship between school personnel and students; the court did not decide whether the district's administrators were actually negligent, and it expressly left open the possible application of statutory immunities. The route to public-entity liability in C.A. is vicarious liability for the negligence of the administrators who did the hiring and supervising, not a direct negligent-hiring claim against the entity; the opinion's discussion of Government Code Section 815 (public-entity liability is exclusively statutory) and of Government Code Section 820 is not restated here. Section 815.2, subdivision (b), which preserves employee immunities, is not quoted. The gendered pronoun in Section 815.2(a) is preserved as written.

TWO-YEAR LIMITATIONS PERIOD FOR PERSONAL INJURY CAUSED BY NEGLECT (CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE SECTION 335.1)
Code of Civil Procedure Section 335.1 provides a two-year period within which to commence an action for assault, battery, or injury to, or for the death of, an individual caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another. A negligent hiring, supervision, or retention claim seeking damages for personal injury or wrongful death is an action for injury caused by the neglect of another within the meaning of this section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "Within two years: An action for assault, battery, or injury to, or for the death of, an individual caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 335.1, Code Civ. Proc. § 335.1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=335.1.)
  Known gap: Section 335.1 states the general personal-injury period only. It does not state when a cause of action accrues, does not address tolling, and does not restate the different periods that other statutes provide for particular claims, for example Code of Civil Procedure Section 340.1 (childhood sexual assault), the claim-presentation requirements of the Government Claims Act that apply before suing a public entity, or the limitations periods for property damage or for statutory claims; none of those is covered in this document. The characterization of a negligent hiring claim as falling within Section 335.1 is a summary of the section's wording rather than a quotation from a decision applying it.

It reflects the statutory and case-law text as of the date checked above and does not reflect any amendments or decisions issued after that date, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

The Restatement (Second) of Agency, which the courts cite as the source of the doctrine, is a secondary source that was not separately fetched for this document; its language is quoted only as reproduced in the published opinions.

expectedJSON.body: In Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church (1992), a case arising from a church's hiring of a youth director, later a pastor, who molested a child parishioner, the California Court of Appeal identified two lines of authority on "negligent hiring" and stated that California follows the view that an employer may be liable to a third person for negligently hiring an incompetent or unfit employee. The court stated that California follows the rule set forth in the Restatement Second of Agency Section 213, under which a person conducting an activity through servants or other agents is subject to liability for harm resulting from his conduct if he is negligent or reckless in the employment of improper persons or instrumentalities in work involving risk of harm to others. Quoting comment d to that section, the court reproduced the Restatement's statements that the principal may be negligent because he has reason to know that the agent, because of his qualities, is likely to harm others in view of the work entrusted to him, that liability results not because of the relation of the parties but because the employer antecedently had reason to believe that an undue risk of harm would exist because of the employment, and that if the work is likely to subject third persons to serious risk of great harm, there is a special duty of investigation. The court summarized the California rule as follows: an employer can be held liable for negligent hiring if he knows the employee is unfit, or has reason to believe the employee is unfit, or fails to use reasonable care to discover the employee's unfitness before hiring him. On the summary-judgment record, the court found a triable issue as to whether the church should have known of the youth director's history and reversed in part.

expectedJSON.gap: Evan F. was decided on a summary-judgment record involving a religious employer and a position entrusted with the care of minors; the opinion also addressed a separate defendant (the church's regional conference), the scope-of-employment question, and other theories not restated here. The Restatement (Second) of Agency Section 213 and its comment d are quoted only as reproduced in the opinion; the Restatement itself was not separately fetched. The opinion's text, as published, contains spacing artifacts within its Restatement quotations (for example, "If. . .the work"), which are not reproduced in the quotation below; the quotation below begins after that fragment. The gendered pronouns in the quoted passages are preserved as written.

expectedJSON.body: In Doe v. Capital Cities (1996), the California Court of Appeal affirmed the dismissal of a negligent hiring, training, and supervision claim brought by an aspiring actor who alleged he was drugged and sexually assaulted by a television network's casting director at the casting director's home. The court stated that California case law recognizes the theory that an employer can be liable to a third person for negligently hiring, supervising, or retaining an unfit employee, and that liability is based upon the facts that the employer knew or should have known that hiring the employee created a particular risk or hazard and that particular harm materializes. The complaint alleged that the employer knew or should have known that the casting director used serious, mind-altering illegal drugs, that he used his position to gain sexual favors, and that use of a "casting couch" is common in the entertainment industry. The court held those allegations insufficient: knowledge that the employee personally used drugs did not equate with knowledge that he would surreptitiously drug a prospective employee and violently assault him, and knowledge that he used his position to extract or coerce sexual favors was not knowledge of the type of conduct alleged. The same opinion separately held that the plaintiff had adequately pleaded a sexual harassment claim under the Fair Employment and Housing Act.

citations.quote: California case law recognizes the theory that an employer can be liable to a third person for negligently hiring, supervising, or retaining an unfit employee.
Liability is based upon the facts that the employer knew or should have known that hiring the employee created a particular risk or hazard and that particular harm materializes.

ABC’s knowledge that Marshall personally used “serious mind-altering drugs” does not equate with knowledge that he would surreptitiously use drugs to place a prospective employee into a situation of helplessness before violently assaulting him.

expectedJSON.gap: Doe v. Capital Cities was decided on demurrer, so the court assessed only the sufficiency of the pleaded allegations; it did not decide what an employer must do to investigate an applicant, and it did not hold that an employer is never liable for an employee's off-premises or off-hours conduct. The opinion's separate FEHA sexual-harassment holding, and its discussion of the relationship between a job applicant and a prospective employer under FEHA, are not restated here. The quotations below are the opinion's own statements of the standard; the first two are frequently reproduced in later opinions (for example, Delfino v. Agilent Technologies and Phillips v. TLC Plumbing, quoted in other clauses of this document).

expectedJSON.body: In Federico v. Superior Court (1997), the California Court of Appeal directed entry of summary judgment for the owner of a hairstyling college who had hired, without a background or reference check, a supervisor with two prior convictions for sexual offenses against young males; the supervisor later molested the minor son of a student after meeting him at the school. Assuming for purposes of review that the owner knew or should have known of the prior convictions and could have foreseen some contact with minors, the court held that hiring the supervisor did not, as a matter of law, breach the employer's limited duty to exercise reasonable care in selecting employees. The court explained that an employer's duty, as defined by California authority and the Restatement, is breached only when the employer knows, or should know, facts which would warn a reasonable person that the employee presents an undue risk of harm to third persons in light of the particular work to be performed. It distinguished Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church on the ground that the pastor there was hired into roles that regularly entrusted him with the care and supervision of minors, whereas the supervisor's position at the hairstyling college required him only to supervise adult students and perform administrative tasks. The court stated that an employer is not charged with guaranteeing the safety of anyone its employee might incidentally meet while on the job against injuries inflicted independent of the performance of work-related functions, and that liability can be imposed only when the employer knows, or should know, that the employee, because of past behavior or other factors, is unfit for the specific tasks to be performed. The court also rejected a negligent-supervision theory because there was no showing that the incidents relied on had been called to the employer's attention or that the employer should have suspected inappropriate behavior on the job.

citations.quote: an employer’s duty, as defined by California authority and the Restatement, is breached only when the employer knows, or should know, facts which would warn a reasonable person that the employee presents an undue risk of harm to third persons in light of the particular work to be performed.

An employer is not charged with guaranteeing the safety of anyone his employee might incidentally meet while on the job against injuries inflicted independent of the performance of work-related functions. Rather, as we have previously explained, liability for negligence can be imposed only when the employer knows, or should know, that the employee, because of past behavior or other factors, is unfit for the specific tasks to be performed.

the contrast between the facts in Evan F. and the present case highlights the significance of the Restatement’s proviso that an employer’s liability must be determined in the context of the specific duties the work entails.

expectedJSON.gap: Federico was decided by writ of mandate on a summary-judgment record and turned on the specific duties of the position at issue; the opinion expressly assumed, without deciding, the employer's knowledge of the prior convictions. The opinion does not address statutory limits on an employer's consideration of criminal history (Labor Code Section 432.7 and the Fair Chance Act, adopted after this decision), which are covered elsewhere in the corpus. The Restatement (Second) of Agency Section 213 and comment d are quoted in the opinion as reproduced from Roman Catholic Bishop v. Superior Court, 42 Cal.App.4th 1556 (1996), which was not separately fetched for this document. The gendered pronoun in the second quotation is preserved as written.

expectedJSON.body: In Delfino v. Agilent Technologies, Inc. (2006), the California Court of Appeal affirmed summary judgment for an employer whose employee had used the employer's computer system to send anonymous threats over the Internet. Restating the standard from Roman Catholic Bishop v. Superior Court, Doe v. Capital Cities, and Evan F. v. Hughson United Methodist Church, the court stated that liability for negligent supervision and/or retention of an employee is one of direct liability for negligence, not vicarious liability. The negligent supervision and retention theory failed for three reasons: it was doubtful, under the factors of Rowland v. Christian, that the employer owed the plaintiffs a duty; even assuming a duty, there was no evidence the employer breached it, because the employer had no knowledge of the content of the employee's threatening messages or of his use of the company system to send them until after the fact, and its internal investigations had not uncovered that use; and even assuming knowledge and inaction, there was no evidence the employee used the employer's system to threaten the plaintiffs after the employer could have acted, so any negligent supervision or retention was not the cause of the claimed injuries.

citations.quote: Liability for negligent supervision and/or retention of an employee is one of direct liability for negligence, not vicarious liability.
Second, even were we to assume the existence of a duty, there was no evidence that Agilent breached any duty of care with respect to the supervision or retention of Moore as an employee.
Thus, any negligent supervision and/or retention of Moore by Agilent—which alleged negligence, as we have concluded, was devoid of factual support—was not the cause of plaintiffs’ claimed injuries.

expectedJSON.gap: Delfino principally decided that the employer was immune under Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act as a provider of an interactive computer service, and also rejected ratification and respondeat superior theories; those holdings are not restated here. The court's duty analysis under Rowland v. Christian was expressed as doubt rather than a definitive holding. The decision concerned supervision and retention of an existing employee rather than the initial hiring decision, and its knowledge and causation reasoning is summarized here because the court treated the negligent hiring, supervision, and retention theories as governed by the same standard.

expectedJSON.body: In Phillips v. TLC Plumbing, Inc. (2009), the California Court of Appeal affirmed summary judgment for a plumbing company sued for negligent hiring and retention after a former service repairman shot and killed a customer he had first met on service calls while employed. The company's owner had learned at hiring that the repairman was on parole and had apparently been convicted of a domestic violence and/or arson offense; the company later terminated him, and the killing occurred about two years after termination. Finding no California case on point, the court surveyed decisions from other jurisdictions applying the Restatement Second of Agency and concluded that, because the employer-employee relationship ends on termination of employment, an employer does not owe a plaintiff a duty of care in a negligent hiring and retention action for harm inflicted by a former employee, even where the former employee initially met the plaintiff while employed. Because the tortious act occurred two years after the employment was terminated, the defendants owed no duty at the time of the act and could not be held liable on the negligent hiring and retention cause of action.

citations.quote: Because the employer-employee relationship ends on termination of an employee’s employment, we conclude an employer does not owe a plaintiff a duty of care in a negligent hiring and retention action for an injury or other harm inflicted by a former employee on the plaintiff even though that former employee, as in this case, initially met the plaintiff while employed by the employer.

because Cain’s tortious act on Judith occurred two years after his employment with TLC was terminated, Defendants did not owe Plaintiff a duty of care at the time of Cain’s tortious act and therefore cannot be held liable on a cause of action for negligent hiring and retention.

expectedJSON.gap: Phillips addressed only whether a duty existed for post-termination conduct; it did not decide whether the initial hiring or the retention of the employee during his employment was negligent, and the opinion offered additional, alternative grounds for the summary judgment that are not restated here. The decision does not address any duty an employer may have under other theories (for example, a duty to warn) and does not address harm inflicted during employment by an employee who is later terminated.

expectedJSON.body: In Diaz v. Carcamo (2011), the California Supreme Court reaffirmed its 1954 decision in Armenta v. Churchill and held that when a plaintiff injured by an employee's negligent driving sues the employer on both respondeat superior and negligent entrustment, hiring, or retention theories, and the employer admits vicarious liability for any negligent driving by its employee, the plaintiff may not continue to pursue the negligent entrustment, hiring, or retention claims. The court described the theory of negligent entrustment as making an employer liable for its own negligence in choosing an employee to drive a vehicle, and stated that an employer's admission of vicarious liability for its employee's negligence makes claims of negligent entrustment, hiring, or retention irrelevant, so that no reason exists to try such claims at all. The court rejected the Court of Appeal's view that this rule had been undermined by California's adoption of comparative fault and by Proposition 51, and it reversed a judgment in which the trial court had admitted evidence of the truck driver's prior accidents and employment history over the employer's objection.

citations.quote: The theory of negligent entrustment makes an employer liable for its own negligence in choosing an employee to drive a vehicle. If, as here, a plaintiff asserts both theories, and the employer admits vicarious liability for any negligent driving by its employee, can the plaintiff still pursue the negligent entrustment claim?

an employer’s admission of vicarious liability for its employee’s negligence makes claims of negligent entrustment, hiring, or retention irrelevant. Thus, no reason exists to try such claims at all, whether separately from the negligence claim or at the same time.

expectedJSON.gap: Diaz arose from a motor-vehicle collision and addressed negligent entrustment, hiring, and retention claims that sought to impose on the employer the same liability as its employee's; the opinion does not address a case in which the employer's own negligence is alleged to have caused harm beyond the employee's negligence, and it does not address intentional torts by employees that fall outside the scope of employment (as in the cases quoted in other clauses of this document), where respondeat superior may be unavailable. The opinion's discussion of comparative fault, Proposition 51, and the specific evidence admitted at trial is not restated here.

expectedJSON.body: Government Code Section 815.2, subdivision (a), provides that a public entity is liable for injury proximately caused by an act or omission of an employee of the public entity within the scope of his employment if the act or omission would, apart from that section, have given rise to a cause of action against that employee. In C.A. v. William S. Hart Union High School District (2012), the California Supreme Court held that a public school district may be vicariously liable under Section 815.2 for the negligence of supervisory or administrative personnel who knew or should have known of a guidance counselor's propensities and nevertheless hired, retained, and inadequately supervised her; the court concluded that the plaintiff's theory of vicarious liability for negligent hiring, retention, and supervision was legally viable, reversing a dismissal on demurrer. The court emphasized that a district's liability must be based on evidence of negligent hiring, supervision, or retention, not on assumptions or speculation, and that an individual school employee's sexual misconduct with a student does not of itself establish, or raise any presumption, that the employing district should bear liability. The court also noted that even when an administrator's negligence is established, the greater share of fault will ordinarily lie with the individual who intentionally abused or harassed the student, which should be reflected in any allocation of comparative fault.

citations.quote: A public entity is liable for injury proximately caused by an act or omission of an employee of the public entity within the scope of his employment if the act or omission would, apart from this section, have given rise to a cause of action against that employee or his personal representative.

citations.case: C.A. v. William S. Hart Union High School District
citations.quote: We conclude plaintiff’s theory of vicarious liability for negligent hiring, retention and supervision is a legally viable one.

citations.case: C.A. v. William S. Hart Union High School District
citations.quote: At the same time, we emphasize that a district’s liability must be based on evidence of negligent hiring, supervision or retention, not on assumptions or speculation. That an individual school employee has committed sexual misconduct with a student or students does not of itself establish, or raise any presumption, that the employing district should bear liability for the resulting injuries.

expectedJSON.gap: C.A. concerned a public school district and rested on the special relationship between school personnel and students; the court did not decide whether the district's administrators were actually negligent, and it expressly left open the possible application of statutory immunities. The route to public-entity liability in C.A. is vicarious liability for the negligence of the administrators who did the hiring and supervising, not a direct negligent-hiring claim against the entity; the opinion's discussion of Government Code Section 815 (public-entity liability is exclusively statutory) and of Government Code Section 820 is not restated here. Section 815.2, subdivision (b), which preserves employee immunities, is not quoted. The gendered pronoun in Section 815.2(a) is preserved as written.

expectedJSON.body: Code of Civil Procedure Section 335.1 provides a two-year period within which to commence an action for assault, battery, or injury to, or for the death of, an individual caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another. A negligent hiring, supervision, or retention claim seeking damages for personal injury or wrongful death is an action for injury caused by the neglect of another within the meaning of this section.

citations.quote: Within two years: An action for assault, battery, or injury to, or for the death of, an individual caused by the wrongful act or neglect of another.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 335.1 states the general personal-injury period only. It does not state when a cause of action accrues, does not address tolling, and does not restate the different periods that other statutes provide for particular claims, for example Code of Civil Procedure Section 340.1 (childhood sexual assault), the claim-presentation requirements of the Government Claims Act that apply before suing a public entity, or the limitations periods for property damage or for statutory claims; none of those is covered in this document. The characterization of a negligent hiring claim as falling within Section 335.1 is a summary of the section's wording rather than a quotation from a decision applying it.
